chapter: Chicago, Villa Venice and Louis Armstrong
title: Moving to Chicago in January 1932 to join Keg
summary: Hinton steers Budd back to his own story; Keg writes from Chicago that musicians there are prosperous, and Budd, who wanted to play with Earl Hines, arrives January 9, 1932.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Well we really dwelled quite a little bit on Booker Pittman, just because he was the grandson of Booker T. Washington, which has so much great black history concerning him. But to get back to Budd Johnson, and the history of Budd Johnson, which we're very much concerned with, we've gotten down to your meeting with Prez, and to your meeting with Coleman Hawkins, and your meeting with Ben Webster, now how -- now you've gotten into -- we didn't get to Chicago yet.
No.
You're still traveling, Budd, and it's 1929 and '30, when you said you came into Chicago with January 9th, 1932. I think you said.
Correct, that is correct.
Yeah, so --
That was with George E. Lee.
Well I was with George E. Lee in '29 and '30: --
Yeah, that's good. That's what I recall.
Is that the band you came -- that you had to make the gig with?
Oh no. Well I left -- you see, now what had happened, my brother had gone into Minneapolis, I

said, and all, and I'd met Prez and everything. Now, my brother had gone on to Chicago. My brother was working now with people like Cass Simpson. Then he finally went into the Regal Theater with Ralph Cooper, and he was working --
Yeah, he --
See, he was in Chicago before me.
Right.

So he wrote me a letter, he says come to Chicago. He said, because here the cats are making a lot of money. He says they're working the theaters in the day, and they're working in the nightclubs in the night, and most of those musicians had their own homes, and everything, and were very prosperous.
And he says, 'You've got to come here.' Well I had been listening --
(Recording interruption.)
-- and most of those musicians had their own homes, and everything, and were very prosperous.

And he says, 'You've got to come here.' Well I had been listening to Earl Hines on the radio, and I had aspired to join that band. I said one of these days I'm going to play with that band. Anyway, January the 9th, 1932 I packed my bags, and took me a train to Chicago, and joined my brother. I didn't have to have any prospects of a job, because my brother said you've got to just come here. I'm making the money,
and you know you come, and I'm staying at so-and-so, you come here and everything, so I was at home. I didn't worry about room rent or eating. And he said, "Get yourself together," and I did.
